script.opening: "I got this letter about my smear test — it says something about HPV and abnormal cells and that I need a ‘colposcopy’. I’ve been in bits since it arrived. Do I have cancer? What does it all mean? And does the HPV thing mean my partner’s cheated, or that I’ve done something?"

facts.text: Arrived 3 days ago. If asked what it says: "high-risk HPV found", "borderline or low-grade changes", and that she will be invited to colposcopy. Hasn’t had the colposcopy appointment through yet.
No bleeding after sex or between periods, no bleeding after periods have finished, no unusual discharge, no pelvic pain. Periods regular. "I feel completely fine — that’s what’s scary."
First smear at 25 was normal. This is her second. Thinks she didn’t have the HPV jab at school ("I was off a lot that year").

facts.topic: Relationship and sexual history (if asked sensitively)
facts.text: With her partner, Leo, for 4 years; before that, two previous partners. Uses the combined pill. No previous STIs. Hasn’t told Leo about the letter yet.
Well; no medicines except the pill; no allergies. Smokes about 5 a day ("I’ve been meaning to stop"). Works as a hairdresser. Not planning a pregnancy right now.
An aunt died of "cancer down below" — Carla isn’t sure if it was cervix or womb. That’s why the letter frightened her so much.

Very anxious, talking quickly, near tears. Calm down noticeably if the doctor starts by explaining clearly that this is not a cancer result. If given jargon (CIN, dyskaryosis) without explanation, look confused and ask what it means. Ask: "So why do I need this colposcopy thing?" and "What do I tell Leo?". Say back the main points at the end if asked.

ice.ideas: "Abnormal cells means cancer. And HPV is an STI, so someone must have given it to me."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — two fears: cancer (her aunt), and her relationship — "Does this mean Leo’s been with someone else? Or he’ll think I have?" She is dreading telling him.
ice.expectations: "To know if I’ve got cancer, and what happens at the colposcopy." Wants to know what to say to her partner.

cues: "Do I have cancer?" — lead with clear reassurance that this is screening, not a cancer diagnosis.
"Does the HPV thing mean my partner’s cheated?" — blame and relationship worry to address without judgement.
"My aunt died of cancer down below" (if asked about worries or family) — why the fear is so strong.

checkpoints.text: Leads with the key reassurance — cervical screening detects high-risk HPV and PRE-cancerous cell changes early; an abnormal screening result is SCREENING, NOT a cancer diagnosis
Explains HPV simply and WITHOUT BLAME — a very common virus, usually cleared, can lie dormant for years, not evidence of promiscuity/infidelity — addressing the relationship question sensitively
Explains that DYSKARYOSIS/CIN is PRE-cancerous (not cancer), that low-grade changes often resolve, and that changes needing treatment are highly treatable — preventing cancer
Explains COLPOSCOPY (magnified look ± biopsy/treatment such as LLETZ, usually quick and awake) and what to expect, framing it as prevention to reduce fear and improve attendance

Reinforces ATTENDING colposcopy and continued screening (5-yearly recall at 25–49 if HPV negative, from 1 July 2025), explains HPV VACCINATION accurately (prevents new infection, doesn’t treat existing HPV; NHS eligibility to the 25th birthday, so not routinely offered at 29), and recognises this is the screening pathway (not a suspected cancer pathway referral) while noting that symptoms need face-to-face examination and a cervix that looks consistent with cancer warrants considering a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Validates her FEAR of cancer and relationship distress, leads with reassurance, and explains a frightening letter in clear, accessible terms
Checks understanding throughout and ensures she leaves reassured, informed and committed to attending — not more frightened

Safety-nets and follows up: the importance of attending colposcopy, what symptoms (abnormal/post-coital bleeding) warrant prompt review, continued screening (HPV vaccine not routinely offered at 29), and support — translating screening abnormality into an understood, supported plan

worked.txt: "Let me put the most important thing first, because I can see you’re terrified: this does NOT mean you have cancer. A cervical screening test is exactly that, a screening test — it’s designed to catch early changes long before they could ever become cancer, so they can be sorted. This is the system working as intended."

"The HPV part — that’s a really common virus that most people who’ve ever been sexually active will have had. It usually clears by itself and can sit silently for years. So finding it does NOT mean your partner’s cheated or that you’ve done anything wrong — please don’t blame yourself or him."

"The ‘abnormal cells’ are pre-cancerous changes — not cancer. Mild ones often go away on their own, and any that need treating are very treatable with a simple procedure. The whole point is to deal with them early so cancer never gets a chance."

"Colposcopy just means a closer look at the cervix with a magnifying camera in a clinic — you’re awake, it’s usually quick. They may take a tiny sample, and if there’s an area that needs it, they can treat it there or soon after. It’s a preventive step, not a scary one."

"The single most important thing is to go to the colposcopy appointment — that’s what keeps you safe. Keep going to your routine cervical screening too. The HPV vaccine prevents new infections rather than treating an existing one, and on the NHS it’s offered up to your 25th birthday, so it isn’t part of your plan now. Does that make the letter make more sense?"

"If you ever get bleeding between periods or after sex, or any new symptoms, tell me — that’s a separate reason to be examined in person. But for now: this is reassuring news caught early, and going to the appointment is the key. I’m here if more questions come up."

f.learning: An abnormal cervical screening result terrifies patients, so lead with the central reassurance: cervical screening is SCREENING, designed to detect high-risk HPV and PRE-CANCEROUS cell changes EARLY so they can be treated before any cancer could develop — an abnormal cervical screening result is NOT a diagnosis of cancer. Explain HPV simply and WITHOUT BLAME: it is a very common sexually-transmitted virus that most sexually active people encounter, usually cleared by the immune system, able to lie DORMANT for years, and finding it does not imply promiscuity or partner infidelity — a frequent, distressing worry to address sensitively. Explain that DYSKARYOSIS (or CIN on biopsy) means abnormal but PRE-cancerous cell changes (not cancer), that low-grade changes often resolve spontaneously, and that changes needing treatment are highly treatable with simple procedures that effectively PREVENT cancer. Explain COLPOSCOPY — a magnified look at the cervix ± a small biopsy and, if needed, treatment (e.g. LLETZ, followed by a test of cure about 6 months later; CIN1 instead has a repeat screening test at 12 months), usually quick and done awake — framing it as prevention and describing what to expect to reduce fear and improve attendance. Reinforce the importance of ATTENDING colposcopy (non-attendance is a key risk), continued routine screening (from 1 July 2025, HPV-negative people aged 25–49 are recalled every 5 years), and accurate HPV VACCINATION information (it prevents new infection but does not treat an existing one; NHS eligibility runs to the 25th birthday, Green Book chapter 18a, so she is outside it at 29), and recognise that this is the cervical-SCREENING pathway (a colposcopy referral), distinct from an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral — though symptoms (abnormal, post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding) need face-to-face examination in their own right, and a cervix whose appearance is consistent with cancer warrants considering a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12). The communication core is fear of cancer and relationship distress; lead with accurate reassurance, explain HPV without blame, demystify colposcopy, validate the fear, check understanding, and ensure she attends.

knowledge.guideline: [1] GOV.UK Cervical screening: programme and colposcopy management (NHS Cervical Screening Programme) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NHS England: cervical screening changes from 1 July 2025 · [3] UKHSA Green Book, chapter 18a (HPV, June 2023) · [5] NHS Digital Cervical Screening Programme, England, colposcopy standards
knowledge.summary: An HPV-positive result with low-grade cell changes is a screening finding, not a cancer diagnosis. Colposcopy looks closer and treats any significant area to prevent cancer. Lead with that, explain HPV without blame, and make sure she attends.

points.t: England uses HPV primary screening: the sample is tested for high-risk HPV first, and only HPV-positive samples are examined for cell changes (cytology). HPV positive with no cell changes: repeat test in 12 months. HPV positive with any cell changes (borderline, low-grade or high-grade dyskaryosis): direct referral to colposcopy [1][2].

NHS England [2]: from 1 July 2025, people aged 25–49 who test HPV negative are recalled every 5 years instead of 3 (50–64 already 5-yearly). Anyone HPV positive within the previous 5 years without a follow-up negative HPV test is recalled sooner before moving to the 5-year interval.

High-risk HPV is very common and usually cleared by the immune system within a couple of years. Dyskaryosis means abnormal cells, not cancer. Low-grade changes often return to normal without treatment. Persistent high-risk HPV is what drives the slow development of pre-cancer (CIN) over years, which is why the programme catches it early.

A clinic examination with a magnifying lens after a speculum is inserted; dilute solutions show abnormal areas, and a small biopsy may be taken. Urgency standard: high-grade referrals are offered an appointment within 2 weeks [5]; low-grade referrals are routine.

NHSCSP [1]: low-grade referral with a normal colposcopy returns to routine recall; biopsy-proven or colposcopic CIN1 has a repeat screening test in the community at 12 months. CIN2 or worse is usually treated, most often by large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), with a test of cure about 6 months after treatment.

Green Book chapter 18a [3]: people who missed the school HPV vaccine remain eligible until their 25th birthday (one dose if under 25). At 29 she is outside routine eligibility. The vaccine prevents new infection and does not treat an existing one, so it does not change her current plan.

NICE NG12 [4]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral if, on examination, the appearance of the cervix is consistent with cervical cancer. Post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding or unusual discharge need examination in their own right, whatever the screening history.

HPV can stay undetectable for years before being picked up, so a positive result cannot show when or from whom it came. It is not evidence of infidelity. Condoms reduce but do not eliminate transmission; there is no routine HPV test for male partners.

Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.

model.text: Hello Miss Nunez, I’m Dr Clarke. Can you hear me okay, and are you somewhere private? … Thank you. What’s been happening?

I got this letter about my smear test. It says something about HPV and abnormal cells and that I need a colposcopy. I’ve been in bits since it arrived. Do I have cancer? What does it all mean? And does the HPV thing mean my partner’s cheated, or that I’ve done something?

I can see how frightening that letter has been. Let me answer the biggest question straight away: this result does not mean you have cancer. I’ll explain exactly what it does mean, and I’ll come back to your partner too. Is that okay?
model.why: Leads with the key reassurance; acknowledges all her questions

model.text: Yes. Please.
Can you read me the exact wording on the letter, so I explain your result and not someone else’s?
model.why: Confirms the actual result before explaining

model.text: It says “high-risk HPV found” and “borderline or low-grade changes” and that I’ll be invited to colposcopy.
Thank you, that matches what I see in your record. Have you had any bleeding between periods or after sex, or any unusual discharge or pain?
model.why: Screens symptoms that would change the pathway

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Have you had an abnormal result before, or been to colposcopy?
Not that I remember.
When you read the letter, what went through your mind?
Cancer. Straight away. And then that someone must have given me something.
That’s a very common reaction, and understandable. What would you most like to leave today knowing?
Whether I’m going to be okay. And what to say to my partner.

The screening test looks first for a virus called HPV. Only if HPV is found does the lab look at the cells. In your sample they found HPV and some mild changes in the cells. Mild changes are not cancer. They’re early changes that often go back to normal by themselves. The whole point of screening is to find them years before anything could become cancer.
model.why: Explains HPV primary screening and low-grade changes accurately

model.text: So why do I need this colposcopy thing?

Because the virus and the changes are both there, the rules are to have a closer look rather than just repeat the test. At colposcopy, a nurse or doctor uses a speculum like a smear, then looks at the cervix through a magnifier. They may take a tiny sample. You’re awake, and it doesn’t usually take long. It’s a preventive check.
model.why: Demystifies colposcopy; explains why referral follows

model.text: And if they find something?

If there’s an area that needs treatment, it’s usually removed with a thin wire loop under local anaesthetic, often at the same or a later visit. Then you’d have a check about six months later. If it’s only mild, they’ll usually just repeat your test in a year. Either way, this is the system catching things early.
model.why: Outlines outcomes: LLETZ with test of cure, or 12-month repeat

model.text: Okay. And my partner?

HPV is extremely common. Most people who have ever had sex will catch it at some point, usually without knowing. It can stay silent for years before a test picks it up, so this result can’t tell us when you caught it or who from. It isn’t a sign that your partner has cheated, or that you’ve done anything wrong.
model.why: Explains HPV latency and removes blame

model.text: That’s a huge relief. I didn’t know what to think.
If it helps, you could tell your partner exactly that: it’s a very common virus that can be carried for years, and the screening is doing its job.
model.why: Offers words for a difficult conversation

model.text: The most important thing is going to the colposcopy appointment. The hospital will contact you directly. If you haven’t heard within a few weeks, ring us and we’ll chase it. Can I ask: is there anything that might make it hard to go?
model.why: Stresses attendance; offers to chase; explores barriers

model.text: Just nerves, really.

That’s normal. You can take someone with you, and you can ask them to stop at any point. The hospital leaflet explains each step as well. One more thing you might read about is the HPV vaccine. It prevents new infections but doesn’t treat an existing one, so it doesn’t change your plan now.
model.why: Practical support; accurate HPV vaccine message

model.text: If before your appointment you notice bleeding after sex or between periods, or an unusual discharge, contact us so we can examine you. Could you tell me in your own words what the result means?
It’s not cancer. I’ve got HPV and mild changes. Colposcopy is a closer look and maybe a small treatment. It doesn’t mean anyone cheated. I need to go.
Perfect. And if more questions come up after we finish, which they often do, book back in with me.
Thank you. I feel so much better.

social.t: HPV results often trigger suspicion of infidelity. Accurate information about latency prevents avoidable harm.
Anxiety and embarrassment are common reasons for missing colposcopy. Explore barriers and offer practical support.

legal.t: Her result is confidential. She chooses what to tell her partner; the GP does not contact partners about HPV.
GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone if she needs a speculum examination for symptoms.

professional.t: The practice should be able to confirm the colposcopy referral has happened; offer to chase if she hears nothing.
Screening intervals changed on 1 July 2025 for 25–49s who test HPV negative. Out-of-date advice creates confusion at recall.

community.t: A well-handled abnormal result supports future attendance, for her and for others she talks to.
The NHS cervical screening pages and cervical cancer charities provide plain-language information about HPV and colposcopy.

redFlags: Cervix that looks suspicious on examination (NICE NG12: consider suspected cancer pathway referral)
psychosocial: Fear of cancer since the letter arrived
Nerves about the procedure and attending
ice: Idea: abnormal smear means cancer; HPV means someone gave her something
Concern: whether she will be okay; the relationship
Expectation: understand the letter and know what to say to her partner

playbook.diagnosis: “Your test found HPV, a very common virus, and some mild changes in the cells of the cervix. This is not cancer. It’s an early change that screening is designed to find.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of screening as a smoke alarm that goes off at the first whiff of toast, long before any fire. Colposcopy is someone coming to check the kitchen. Most of the time it’s just toast.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought straight away that this meant cancer, and wondered whether your partner had cheated. Neither is what this result shows.”
management.psychosocial: Give her words for the partner conversation; address nerves about colposcopy; open door for questions after she has read the leaflet.
sharedPlan: Attend colposcopy: the hospital will invite her directly; practice will chase if no contact
Colposcopy: closer look ± small biopsy; LLETZ if CIN2 or worse, then test of cure at about 6 months
If only mild changes: repeat screening test at 12 months
HPV vaccine not indicated now at 29 and does not treat current infection
safetyNet: Contact the practice for bleeding after sex or between periods, or unusual discharge
Ring if no colposcopy appointment arrives

pitfalls.intro: The trap is explaining the science before answering her real question. Marks sit in answering “is it cancer?” first, explaining HPV without blame, and securing attendance.

items.fail: Starting with the biology of HPV and CIN before answering “do I have cancer?”
items.why: She cannot absorb anything while that question is unanswered.
items.fix: “This result does not mean you have cancer.” Then explain.

items.why: England uses HPV primary screening; cytology is only read when HPV is found.
items.fix: “The test looks for HPV first, then at the cells.”

items.fail: Advising the HPV vaccine as treatment.
items.why: She is outside NHS eligibility at 29 and the vaccine doesn’t clear an existing infection.
items.fix: Explain that it prevents new infections only.

items.fail: Ignoring or rushing the partner question.
items.why: It is her hidden agenda and a source of real harm.
items.fix: Explain HPV latency and offer words she can use.
Reassure accurately and stress that attending is what keeps her safe.

items.fail: No plan if the appointment doesn’t arrive, and no symptom safety-net.
items.why: Lost referrals and new symptoms are the real risks.
items.fix: Offer to chase; name post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding.

timeMap.d: She asks if she has cancer. Answer that first, then promise to return to her other questions.
Exact letter wording, bleeding or discharge, previous abnormal results.
Cancer fear, the relationship worry, what she wants to leave knowing.
HPV primary screening, mild changes, why colposcopy, what happens there, possible outcomes, HPV and blame.
Attendance, chasing, barriers, HPV vaccine accuracy, symptom safety-net, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Explains pathology jargon without first answering “do I have cancer?”; implies HPV reflects sexual behaviour; tells her to get the HPV vaccine now; no emphasis on attending colposcopy.
wordPics.pass: Reassures that this is not cancer, explains HPV and low-grade changes, describes colposcopy, stresses attending and safety-nets for bleeding.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: answers the cancer question in the first minute; explains how HPV primary screening works; addresses the partner question with HPV latency and gives her words to use; outlines LLETZ, test of cure and 12-month repeat; knows the 2025 interval change and vaccine eligibility; offers to chase the appointment; teach-back.

avoid.instead: “It isn’t cancer. It’s an early change that the screening is designed to catch, and the next step is a closer look.”
avoid.why: Vague reassurance may lead her to skip colposcopy.

avoid.dont: “HPV is a sexually transmitted infection, so you’ll need to talk to your partner.”
avoid.instead: “HPV is extremely common and can stay silent for years, so this can’t show when you caught it or from whom.”
avoid.why: Framing HPV as a recent STI fuels blame and relationship harm.

avoid.dont: “You should get the HPV jab now.”
avoid.instead: “The vaccine prevents new infections but doesn’t treat an existing one, so it doesn’t change your plan now.”
avoid.why: She is outside NHS eligibility (to 25th birthday) and it would not treat her current infection.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An HPV-positive result with low-grade cell changes is a screening finding, not a cancer diagnosis. Colposcopy looks closer and treats any significant area to prevent cancer. Lead with that, explain HPV without blame, and make sure she attends.

points.t: England uses HPV primary screening: the sample is tested for high-risk HPV first, and only HPV-positive samples are examined for cell changes (cytology). HPV positive with no cell changes: repeat test in 12 months. HPV positive with any cell changes (borderline, low-grade or high-grade dyskaryosis): direct referral to colposcopy [1][2].

NHS England [2]: from 1 July 2025, people aged 25–49 who test HPV negative are recalled every 5 years instead of 3 (50–64 already 5-yearly). Anyone HPV positive within the previous 5 years without a follow-up negative HPV test is recalled sooner before moving to the 5-year interval.

High-risk HPV is very common and usually cleared by the immune system within a couple of years. Dyskaryosis means abnormal cells, not cancer. Low-grade changes often return to normal without treatment. Persistent high-risk HPV is what drives the slow development of pre-cancer (CIN) over years, which is why the programme catches it early.

A clinic examination with a magnifying lens after a speculum is inserted; dilute solutions show abnormal areas, and a small biopsy may be taken. Urgency standard: high-grade referrals are offered an appointment within 2 weeks [5]; low-grade referrals are routine.

NHSCSP [1]: low-grade referral with a normal colposcopy returns to routine recall; biopsy-proven or colposcopic CIN1 has a repeat screening test in the community at 12 months. CIN2 or worse is usually treated, most often by large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), with a test of cure about 6 months after treatment.

Green Book chapter 18a [3]: people who missed the school HPV vaccine remain eligible until their 25th birthday (one dose if under 25). At 29 she is outside routine eligibility. The vaccine prevents new infection and does not treat an existing one, so it does not change her current plan.

NICE NG12 [4]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral if, on examination, the appearance of the cervix is consistent with cervical cancer. Post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding or unusual discharge need examination in their own right, whatever the screening history.

HPV can stay undetectable for years before being picked up, so a positive result cannot show when or from whom it came. It is not evidence of infidelity. Condoms reduce but do not eliminate transmission; there is no routine HPV test for male partners.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy; open question; let her voice all three questions.
Relationship worry and distress since the letter explored without judgement.
Picked up “does the HPV thing mean my partner’s cheated?” and returned to it.
Idea (cancer; someone gave her something), concern (being okay; the relationship), expectation (to understand and know what to say to her partner).
Confirmed the exact result wording; screening history; symptom check for bleeding or discharge.
Screening abnormality vs symptomatic disease; knows NICE NG12 applies only to a suspicious-looking cervix.
Screened post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding and discharge; knows high-grade referrals are seen within 2 weeks.
High-risk HPV with low-grade changes: screening abnormality, not cancer.
Colposcopy explained; LLETZ and test of cure or 12-month repeat outlined; offer to chase the appointment.
Barriers to attending explored; partner conversation supported; accurate HPV vaccine message at 29.
Symptom safety-net before colposcopy; chase if no appointment; open door for later questions.

social.t: HPV results often trigger suspicion of infidelity. Accurate information about latency prevents avoidable harm.
Anxiety and embarrassment are common reasons for missing colposcopy. Explore barriers and offer practical support.

legal.t: Her result is confidential. She chooses what to tell her partner; the GP does not contact partners about HPV.
GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone if she needs a speculum examination for symptoms.

professional.t: The practice should be able to confirm the colposcopy referral has happened; offer to chase if she hears nothing.
Screening intervals changed on 1 July 2025 for 25–49s who test HPV negative. Out-of-date advice creates confusion at recall.

community.t: A well-handled abnormal result supports future attendance, for her and for others she talks to.
The NHS cervical screening pages and cervical cancer charities provide plain-language information about HPV and colposcopy.

redFlags: Cervix that looks suspicious on examination (NICE NG12: consider suspected cancer pathway referral)
psychosocial: Fear of cancer since the letter arrived
Nerves about the procedure and attending
ice: Idea: abnormal smear means cancer; HPV means someone gave her something
Concern: whether she will be okay; the relationship
Expectation: understand the letter and know what to say to her partner

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your test found HPV, a very common virus, and some mild changes in the cells of the cervix. This is not cancer. It’s an early change that screening is designed to find.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of screening as a smoke alarm that goes off at the first whiff of toast, long before any fire. Colposcopy is someone coming to check the kitchen. Most of the time it’s just toast.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought straight away that this meant cancer, and wondered whether your partner had cheated. Neither is what this result shows.”
management.psychosocial: Give her words for the partner conversation; address nerves about colposcopy; open door for questions after she has read the leaflet.
sharedPlan: Attend colposcopy: the hospital will invite her directly; practice will chase if no contact
Colposcopy: closer look ± small biopsy; LLETZ if CIN2 or worse, then test of cure at about 6 months
If only mild changes: repeat screening test at 12 months
HPV vaccine not indicated now at 29 and does not treat current infection
safetyNet: Contact the practice for bleeding after sex or between periods, or unusual discharge
Ring if no colposcopy appointment arrives

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is explaining the science before answering her real question. Marks sit in answering “is it cancer?” first, explaining HPV without blame, and securing attendance.

items.fail: Starting with the biology of HPV and CIN before answering “do I have cancer?”
items.why: She cannot absorb anything while that question is unanswered.
items.fix: “This result does not mean you have cancer.” Then explain.

items.why: England uses HPV primary screening; cytology is only read when HPV is found.
items.fix: “The test looks for HPV first, then at the cells.”

items.fail: Advising the HPV vaccine as treatment.
items.why: She is outside NHS eligibility at 29 and the vaccine doesn’t clear an existing infection.
items.fix: Explain that it prevents new infections only.

items.fail: Ignoring or rushing the partner question.
items.why: It is her hidden agenda and a source of real harm.
items.fix: Explain HPV latency and offer words she can use.
Reassure accurately and stress that attending is what keeps her safe.

items.fail: No plan if the appointment doesn’t arrive, and no symptom safety-net.
items.why: Lost referrals and new symptoms are the real risks.
items.fix: Offer to chase; name post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding.
